anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between tables, indexes, partitions, data types, or constraints and the workload, forcing queries into full scans, non-covering lookups, or unbalanced partition access.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Unbounded or badly sized buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and session heaps that push the host into sustained memory pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion of free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas, leading to allocation failures, auto-extend errors, and stalled write or sort operations.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the engine exhibits a cascade of symptoms: full-table scans triggered by poor indexing inflate the amount of pages pulled into the buffer cache and enlarge per-query hash/sort work areas, accelerating memory growth; once memory is saturated, these operations spill to temporary segments, which rapidly erode remaining disk space and provoke temp-file or tablespace full errors; concurrent paging, swap thrashing, and temp-space saturation magnify I/O latency, so even simple OLTP statements and maintenance tasks stall, while log files and backups cannot grow or rotate, risking transaction blockage and recovery gaps.

Causally, inefficient schema design is the first amplifier—forcing wide data reads that demand large memory and temp resources. The enlarged memory footprint hastens the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly; under pressure, the engine spills intermediate results to disk, directly feeding the Storage Space Capacity Anomaly. Conversely, dwindling disk space prevents further temp spills or index creation, forcing more in-memory work that exacerbates memory exhaustion. This positive feedback loop between design-induced I/O, runaway memory use, and shrinking storage surfaces as a compounded, hard-to-diagnose performance and availability degradation that is far more severe than any of the three issues in isolation.

entry.error_class: Class 42 - Syntax Error or Access Rule Violation
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with unsupported syntax, invalid statement structure, or feature usage that the target engine version cannot execute as written.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate SQL syntax, target-engine compatibility, statement shape, and whether the feature is supported under the current engine version or execution context.
